speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The question is on the amendment of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to clause 4.

On clause 4 last evening
a general discussion arose and a statement was made by the leader of the opposition to the effect that Sir Henry Thornton had been forced out of his directorship in the Royal Bank by the action of this government. That, in brief, was the gist of the remarks made by the right hon. gentleman. I denied the statement at the time and he persisted m it, saying that he 'had been so informed by Sir Henry Thornton and believed him. This morning I made some inquiries, the result of which I wish to put on record merely

C.N.R.-CJP.R. Bill
to keep the record reasonably straight. I find that Sir Henry Thornton was appointed a Royal Bank director on December 10, 1929, when the right hon. gentleman still had some considerable time to go before he went out of poiwer. Sir Henry was reelected a director of the Royal Bank on January 9, 1930, again on January 8, 1931, and again on January 14, 1932. He remained a director until the annual meeting of January 12, 1933, at which meeting he was not reelected. However, he had resigned the presidency of the Canadian National Railways on July 19, 1932, so that he was a director of the Royal Bank for six months after he had resigned from the presidency of the Canadian National Railways. May I suggest, without going any further, that these facts constitute a complete answer to the right hon. gentleman's charge that this government in some way influenced the Royal Bank to make Sir Henry Thornton withdraw from the directorate of that institution. That in itself is proof enough without anything further, although I have a little further proof if I need it.

May I say to my hon. friend that Sir Henry Thornton was certainly under the impression-and he so informed me-that the reason he was not reappointed on the board of directors of the Royal Bank was due to the action of the Dominion government. I assumed at the time that this was because of his being also president of the road. In that I may have misunderstood the significance of his not being retained as a director. This, however, would only make the situation more aggravating, because it would indicate that the government was interfering with a purely private business in the appointment of a director of a private corporation. But Sir Henry Thornton certainly had the impression that the reason he was not reappointed was that the bank had intimated to him that he must resign and the intimation conveyed with it the impression that the government of the day had considered that advisable.

The right hon. gentleman's remarks to-day are a good deal milder than his observations of last night. He said then that Sir Henry Thornton had told him that and he believed what Sir Henry Thornton had said.
I do.

I shall give my right hon. friend still further proof that the statement is not true. I have under my hand a telegram
from Mr. M. W. Wilson, general manager, and,
I think, vice-president of the Royal Bank of Canada. I telegraphed to him, asking about the matter, and this is his reply:	'
Your telegram received. When Sir Henry Thornton retired from the Canadian National Railways he offered to resign from the board of this bank but it was suggested that he allow the matter to stand until his future plans became more definite. As you are aware he subsequently removed to New York and shortly before our annual meeting in January he intimated that as he was no longer a resident of Canada he did not wish to offer himself for reelection. His wishes were carried out. At no time was the question of his directorship discussed with us by any member of the government.

May I ask the minister whether he can and will say that Sir Henry Thornton's intimation that he was not to be renominated was not due to a message which was sent by Mr. Wilson himself to his manager in New York who convened it to Sir Henry and that when it was conveyed to him, he intimated that under the circumstances he would not expect to be reappointed?

I do not know anything about any private messages of Mr. Wilson to Sir Henry Thornton. I have given a public message from Mr. Wilson to the people of Canada. I accept Mr. Wilson's word. Furthermore, last night I made the statement- and I repeat it to-day-that the government had nothing whatever to do with Sir Henry Thornton's retiring from the board of directors of the Royal Bank. Moreover, if the right hon. gentleman were fair, which he is not, he would accept that statement and withdraw his own.
I have given to my hon. friend the reasons why Sir Henry Thornton believed that he was being asked to retire from that board at the instance of the government.
He was making excuses for the fact that he was dropped, probably.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think we had perhaps better come back to the question. The question is on the amendment to clause 4. An amendment has also been moved by Mr. Elliott and withdrawn for the time being. Does the hon. member wish to press his amendment?

I thought the arrangement last night was that it would be considered with the amendment to section 11, as the two relate to practically the same thing.
C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill

May I say, Mr. Chairman, that there is no doubt that we shall not get through this bill to-day because the acting leader of the government stated last evening that we should not go on with it probably beyond five o'clock, and it is not at all likely that we shall get through with it before then because there are still quite a number of clauses to consider, but I will make this statement now with respect to clauses 11 and 7, both of which are in dispute, that we shall not deal with them to-day. I should like, however, to go on and make progress with some of the other clauses. The passage of the amendment which has been moved by my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce would not interfere with section 11 at all in so far as the hon. gentleman desires to amend section 11.
I made the statement last night that we had been three weeks on this bill, and I was corrected by the leader of the opposition. I have made inquiries to-day and had the reflbrd searched, and I find that we have spent fifteen actual working days on the bill, or exactly three full weeks of five days a week, and it is seven weeks since we introduced the bill. I should like to make some progress to-day and go on with section 4. We are quite agreeable to allowing sections 7 and 11 to stand until next week.
Does the minister contemplate any amendment to section 7?
No.
The minister will have to shorten his speeches to make headway.
Perhaps the right hon. gentleman might take a little of that himself.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: In order to put the question clearly before the committee I might stale that the hon. member for West Middlesex moved an amendment to clause 4 which was withdrawn to allow the committee to discuss the new subclause 2. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has moved an amendment which will be subclause 3 of clause 4 if adopted. Does the hon. member for West Middlesex wish to press his amendment?
I am afraid that the minister is not shortening the debate by separating this clause from the proposed amendment to section 11.
I do not quite follow. Would the hon. member explain the connection between the two, and why we cannot proceed to pass clause 4?

This amendment deals with the question whether or not all the trustees shall be full-time men. The amendment proposed to section 11 deals with the question of whether all the trustees shall have equal voting power. I say that the two affect so vitally the effectiveness of the board of trustees, and are so closely connected, that I think it would save time to consider them both together, and that was the understanding given.

I just want to get straight what my hon. friend means. I do not quite see what difference it would make to proceed now with section 4. I have met my hon. friend's wishes to a large extent in the amendment which we have moved. We have now moved two amendments, one about the chairman and directorships and so on, and the other in regard to the other two trustees. These other two trustees at the discretion of the governor in council may also be full-time men, so I think I have practically met my hon. friend's wishes so far as full-time trustees go. In regard to the question of a majority vote, that is a separate question altogether, and I suggest with all respect that we can deal with that when we come to it. Here is the government's submission in regard to section 4. I think we might pass that, and I am quite ready to hold sections 7 and 11 over till next week. It seems to me that the two questions are separate and distinct.

As I explained to my hon. friend last night, the amendment moved by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce will not, I submit, be of any great benefit if the vote of the other two trustees can only be counted when the bhairman votes with either one of them. I do not want to be disrespectful with regard to the amendment that has been proposed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I realize that it is a step in the right direction, but it is only a step, I submit, providing that the trustees are what I would call real trustees, operative trustees, having a vote of equal weight on the board with the chairman. I do submit that we will save time by considering them together, and that was agreed to last night.

I am very anxious to
oblige, although it has not done me very much good so far. At the same time I do not yet see any connection between the two.
I know what the hon. gentleman has in mind, but so far as section 4 is concerned we are taking this attitude irrespective of what we do with section 11. I think my hon. friend might therefore concede that we have gone

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill
a long way with him on this. So now let us dispose of it, and then when we come to section 11 we can argue the question whether there should be a majority vote or not.

I am not going to occupy more of the time of the committee in arguing whether we should consider this amendment now or later. Unless we can fallow the arrangement that was made last night I must submit the amendment which I moved before.
That is all right; go ahead and submit the amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Elliott moves that all the words after the word "that" in the proposed amendment to be known as subsection 3 of clause 4 be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
One of such trustees shall be their chairman. Each trustee shall devote his whole time to the performance of the duties of his office and shall not be an officer of any company other than a company which is comprised in National railways and shall not, during his tenure of office as trustee, become a director of any company other than a company which is comprised in National railways of which he was not a director at the time of his appointment.

Before the vote is taken may I call the attention of the committee to what that means. I assume that they have it pretty well in their minds. This is a very, very important board. They have to administer a property of the people of this country which has cost and is worth many millions of dollars. It will be perhaps the most important board functioning in the dominion, and I submit that what was formerly done by a board of seventeen on the Canadian National Railways, and by a board of about an equal number on the Canadian Pacific Railway, is of sufficient importance and sufficiently onerous to demand the whole time of three of the very best men that can be obtained. That is the object of the amendment. I do not think that this great national asset should be entrusted to three men any one of whom should be permitted to give only part of his time to that work.

I agree with the hon. gentleman. He has explained his amendment quite correctly, but we have made an amendment whereby the governor in council may, at discretion, make all three trustees full-time men. I stated last night, and I repeat now, that as far as I know it is the intention of the government to do that for a time at least, so I am sorry to have to refuse to accept the hon. gentleman's amendment. I shall have to vote against it.

This is a very important question. When the bill was before the house before the Easter recess, I had intended moving an amendment that the board of trustees be enlarged from three to five members. I wish to protest against the board being limited to three members. The maritime provinces claim that under the British North America Act they have certain rights which they look to this and all governments to protect. We feel that if a board of trustees consisting of only three members is chosen from central Canada the claims of the maritime provinces may be overlooked. Under the terms of the legislation the trustees have great powers. They may scrap lines or cut down services. In the report of the Duncan commission there is the following finding regarding the old Intercolonial railway:
That to the extent that commercial considerations were subordinate to national, imperial and strategic considerations, the cost would be borne by the dominion and not by the traffic that might pass over the line.
If the trustees put that line on a strictly paying basis, and curtail services until that object is reached, I claim that they will not be playing fair with the maritime provinces, and will not be adhering to the terms set out at confederation. I do not know whether there are to be three or five members, but if I were in order I should feel very much like moving an amendment to the effect that there should be five trustees, one of whom should come from the maritime provinces.
You have a great chance of getting it.
Question.

On the
point of order-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

But I

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

Mr. Chairman, in my opinion the ruling of the chair is correct. I certainly understood that in dealing with this bill we are not following ordinary rules, passing it section by section, but subsection by subsection. There were to be three, appointed for seven years; now we have three men who are to be appointed practically during pleasure, who may be removed from time to time, and may be employed for part time or full time or any time at all. I am not quarrelling with the amendment, but I say that if you have entirely changed the duties of the trustees then it is competent for any member to propose that there shall be five instead of three.

There is one matter on which I am not very clear, which I think can be brought up under any section in part I, which refers to the national railways. According to section 3 (d) "National company" means the Canadian National Railway Company. Then in subsection (e) I find the following:
"National railways" means the National company, as owner, operator, manager or otherwise, and its transportation, communication and hotel system, which system shall be deemed to comprise all companies which are elements of the Canadian National Railways as defined in the National act-
I should like to know if this act is sufficiently broad to include the Canadian Government Merchant Marine and the Canadian National Steamship Company. If it is I have nothing more to say, but if it is not I think some clause should be included providing that the three trustees who are to take over the Canadian National Railways shall take over the merchant marine and national steamships as well. If that is not done it will mean, that the minister or the government will have to retain the present directors, or others, to look after the affairs of those two companies. So I think we might as well arrange that the trustees to be appointed under this act should also look after the affairs of these two companies instead of having two separate companies looking after the business of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine and the Canadian National Steamship Company.

I agree entirely with the
hon. gentleman, but that provision is not in the bill because it is not necessary. The Canadian National steamships and the Canadian Government Merchant Marine are entrusted to the same directorate by order in council. I confess that the matter has not been discussed, but I am quite sure it is the intention of the government to have these companies looked after in future as they have been looked after in the past. I quite agree that there would be no reason for having a separate board of directors, but that matter can be dealt with by order in council, so it need not form part of the act.

Unless it is in the act I do not see how the governor in council can decide that these two companies do come under this act. This bill is very specific; it deals with certain matters, and according to the definition in subsection (e) of section 3 it would not include the two companies I have mentioned. It seems to me that I have a strong argument, and I think the minister agrees that the Canadian Government Merchant Marine and the Canadian National steamships should be handled by the trustees who are to be appointed under this bill. I think before we pass this bill an amendment should be moved, or a new clause added, so that the trustees appointed under this act will manage not only the railway company but the merchant marine and the National steamships as well. I cannot agree with the minister that in some way the governor in council can arrange to place the merchant marine and the National steamships under this act, by order in council, giving the three trustees power to manage those companies. It would be a very simple matter to make that provision; for instance, the definition contained in subsection (e) of section 3 might be enlarged to include the Canadian Government Merchant Marine and the Canadian National Steamship Company. I think the minister agrees that there should be only one management for the three companies, and I think it would be an easy matter to make that clear now.

I very largely agree with the idea that the management of the merchant marine and the steamship company should be as the hon. member suggests, but in the past these companies were not entrusted to the directors of the Canadian National. By order in council the directors of the National railways were simply made directors of these two companies as well; they were not so appointed under any act, and I submit that it is not necessary to put them under this act. However, I hardly think we will finish this bill to-day, and I will agree that before we do so I will give a fuller explanation to my hon. friend than I have given at the moment, if that will be satisfactory.
That will be quite satisfactory.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The first question to be dealt with by the committee is the amendment of the hon. member for Quebec South, who moved that the section be amended by striking out all the words after the word "occurring" in the fourteenth line.
C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill
Would the bon. gentleman just explain what he has in mind?

The effect would be that in future the appointments would be made by order in council, and we would do away with this panel system. I think the minister agreed to a certain extent that if the original trustees were to be appointed by order in council there was no reason why those succeeding them should not be appointed in the same way. The panel system seems a rather cumbersome method of going about it.

I agree that there is a good deal to be said in favour of the suggestion of the hon. member, but at the same time after a good deal of discussion the government thought this was the better way to leave it, on the ground that, speaking broadly, the panel system is a more non-political method of dealing with the question than appointment by order in council, whether under this or another government. It is true that at the present time the government is appointing the three trustees but for the future it is recommended that if one trustee disappears, the president of the Exchequer court and the chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners and the remaining trustees may submit a panel of eight names. I do not know that there is every protection against political manoeuvring, if whatever government happens to be in power chooses to manoeuvre, but it is considered that it would be better to leave the panel proposal in the bill.

I submit that the argument just advanced by the minister is not very strong. This government will appoint three trustees and under the panel system those trustees may be self-perpetuating. There is no question but that they can arrange for their own reappointment. The three men will be able to run this railroad for eternity, if it lasts that long. There is another viewpoint which perhaps should be considered when considering the amendment of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Under that amendment, these trustees need not be appointed for a definite term. They can be appointed for part time service and then for full time service if the governor in council deems it advisable. It might very well happen that these appointments would not be made definite or permanent until this government was about to go out of office, at which time the trustees would have had five, six or seven years of service, as the case may be. It seems to me that if the government wished to be fair it would say that the original appointments shall be made from a panel. I think they [The Chairman.]
should either say that or say that all future appointments will be made by the governor in council. I cannot see any force in the minister's argument that we are getting away from politics.

I shall touch upon only one point raised by the hon. gentleman. When we reach the clause covering that matter, it is the intention of the government to move an amendment in order to make the appointments definite as to years. We would not be able to put through the rather "slick" game the hon. gentleman suggests. We intend to make the appointment for seven, six and five years or five, four and three as may be decided by the committee.

I would like to get an interpretation of the new clause number three to section 4, which reads:
The trustees, other than the chairman, first appointed under the provisions of this act shall from time to time during the terms of their appointments devote to performance of the duties of their office their whole or part time as may be determined from time to time by the governor in council, and the salaries to be paid to such trustees for whole and/or part time service shall be fixed at the time of their appointments.
I see nothing in that clause to prevent the government making these part time appointments to date from the date of appointment and then some fine day making them full time appointments, say for a period of five years.

I think my hon. friend is
putting a fairly loose interpretation upon that clause. The reason this clause was drawn up by the legal officers of the Department of Justice and my department was in order-

I know why it was drawn
up.

It was not drawn up for
the purpose suggested by the hon. gentleman.
I am not imputing motives.

The first appointments
might be made for seven years for the chairman, six years for one of the trustees and five for the other, but if we decided to put them in for full time, say for the first three years, under clause 7 we could not interfere with them without an address of both houses of parliament. We could not undo the work we had done, that is, we could not change their salaries or anything of that sort without an address of both houses of parliament. I may say quite frankly that when we get to

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill
the next clause and decide upon the term of the appointment, we will not be able to go outside of that provision by making them part time for a portion of their term and full time for another portion.

I suppose it is pretty much wasting time to make any suggestions in view of the fact that the minister has stated that the government intends to stand by this clause as it is now worded. Apparently.it is the intention of the government to provide for the panel method of selection in the case of vacancies, and it is stated that this is done to avoid the possibility of political appointments. It does not seem to me that this provision meets the case at all. As I pointed out on the second reading of the bill, if this is an efficient method of guarding against political appointments to fill future vacancies, the same plan should be followed in appointing the original board. We should be consistent. Let us assume that it is the desire of the government to control this board politically. It will appoint three men who are amenable to government influence. I am presupposing and not charging this. Should a vacancy occur, the two trustees remaining will no doubt renominate themselves upon the panel, while the president of the exchequer court and the chairman of the railway board will make certain other selections for the same panel.
Eight names.

There will be eight names
altogether. The point I want to make is that the two men left on that board, being politicians-the committee knows the sense in which I use that word-will no doubt select four other politicians for their portion of the panel. The president of the exchequer court and the chairman of the railway board may select four men whom they think are not tarnished with political feeling, but if the government wants to do so they can ignore entirely those four nominees. If the first appointments are political-they certainly can be although I do not say they will be-this board will be able to perpetuate itself as a political organization. It seems to me that the provision of having the president of the exchequer court and the chairman of the railway board submit four names to the panel is absolutely useless because the government could ignore those names entirely. If I am wrong in this assumption, I should like to be placed right. The government is not enjoined or compelled to select any name from those submitted by the president of the court and the chairman of the board; if they wish they
can fill the vacancy from the trustees who are still left on the board. I suppose it would be more than human nature to expect that these two men would not put their own names upon the panel and be again selected. If this method is to be adopted at all, I would like to see it adopted right from the beginning. If the panel principle is going to get rid of politics, then I think it ought to be applied in the first instance. If we start out on a political basis-I am assuming that in order to make my argument-the thing will perpetuate itself.

Supposing the government was the same one that appointed the three; then a panel of eight names was submitted, if the government wished to replace two or three of them, irrespective of the other five or six, the government could do so. But supposing in the meantime the government had changed, the trustees could not submit their own names in any way I know of, where the new government would not have the opportunity of replacing them if it so desired.
If the government changed, they might take the selections submitted by the two trustees.
But they could refuse them altogether; after all, parliament is supreme.
The whole thing, it seems to me, is imperfect.

I am not arguing its perfection, I will admit. It was suggested by the royal commission that in the case of a vacancy a panel be submitted by the two remaining trustees. That was their reason for the "stagger" system in the appointments, so that one at a time would drop out and the other two would submit a panel. But in order that there might be a broader basis for the selection of a panel, there were added to the selectors, if I may use that word, the president of the exchequer court and the chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners. I may say quite frankly that the question was discussed whether the government of the day could not put on a representative, but that would make the matter still more political. The general recommendation of the royal commission being as I have said, the government decided to insert it in the bill.

Does the government not think it is a most remarkable principle to ask men who are already on the board to make selections for the panel? It seems to me that they are prejudiced and self-interested, that
C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill

is if they wish to act in that way, and it would be better to have the selections made by others than those who are already on the board. What is the principle that governs that provision?

Is that not provided for in the fact that the chairman of the railway commission and the president of the exchequer court can also submit names? It is not possible for the two trustees to submit eight names. They would probably submit four and the others would submit four, so that the government would probably have a voice, and the selection would not really prejudice whichever party happened to be in power.

Why should the two surviving trustees be selected to submit the four names? Are they the proper persons to do that sort of work? If they are prejudiced, as they well might be, why not somebody else instead of those two?

An argument may be advanced in this regard, but there is this to be said for the two remaining trustees; they would understand the railway business to a certain extent and they would know the type of men who should be selected. We will take it for granted that they are honest and true men, and they will probably submit names of men that will be of a suitable type. They might desire to be selected themselves, but the two men submitting the names are not in the panel to be selected. They remain. The submission of a panel is only in the case of one trustee dropping out, because they drop out according to the "stagger" system. They do not submit their own names, and, having iad some understanding of the railway business, they should be able to select the right type of men for the position.

The minister is on
extremely weak ground in the action he is taking. The government say that the first three trustees are to be appointed by the governor in council and there should be some reason for taking away from it the power to appoint in the case of a vacancy. If the governor in council is good enough to appoint the first board, when the time comes for these men to be replaced, the governor in council should be equally competent to appoint their successors. I do not see why the government should want to get away from this practice which has always been followed in making appointments. In this case I think the government is trying to put over the house this bill which is extreme in many ways, and then to appoint a self-selecting board of

trustees to carry on in defiance of another party that may happen to be in power is most unfair. The minister is on weak ground in presenting such an argument.

Is it in the minister's
mind-it may be a question of legal interpretation-that the nominating board, so-called, should be unanimous in selecting a panel, or is a majority sufficient? Possibly the remaining trustees might make certain selections and the president of the exchequer court and the chairman of the railway board might act as if they were making individual nominations. I take it that the nominations are by a board and I am wondering whether a majority of the board is sufficient or whether it must be unanimous.

I do not think that has
been discussed, but the government takes it for granted that the two trustees remaining, the president of the exchequer court and the chairman of the board of railway commissioners would unanimously submit a, panel of eight. The clause says that if any such panel of eight is not submitted within ten days in the case of a vacancy, the governor in council may appoint as he may be advised. I am quite frank in saying that it would be difficult for a panel to be submitted in ten days, so that whatever government might be in power, it would likely find itself forced to make the appointments anyway.
Does the minister think the period of ten days might be increased to twenty or thirty?

If the hon. member does
not like the way in which the panel is appointed, why not move to wipe out the ten day provision?

My hon. friend states that this is the recommendation of the royal commission and that for this reason it has been inserted. The royal commission have made several recommendations that have not been .inserted. Its members have given their recommendations from their point of view, but we are here as parliament to legislate from our point of view. I should not like to be a party to a reflection by legislation on the government of the day, no matter what government it might be. I am speaking to my political opponents, and I say that I have much more faith in their judgment in making appointments to this board than in the judgment of the president of the exchequer court and the chairman of the board of railway commissioners, however able those gentlemen may be. Ministerial responsibility is the

C.N.B.-C.P.R. Bill
basis of security so far as the public is concerned. Whatever the royal commission may recommend, I do not think it is fitting for parliament impliedly to reflect upon any present or future administration, and this is what is being done by the section as it stands. The intention is good no doubt. There is nothing to prevent the government, if it so wishes, from calling in the president of the exchequer court and the chairman of the board of railway commissioners and consulting them; in fact, that is exactly what the government would do if it believed they were in a position to advise, but security in the matter of appointments rests in keeping them under ministerial responsibility, not in getting away from it. Surely if the government can appoint the judges of the country; if it can appoint these very gentlemen, the president of the exchequer court and the chairman of the railway commission, if it can appoint the personnel of all the other commissions, it can make equally fair and good appointments in the case of the trustees? Why, just beqause we have in the case of the Canadian National Railways a commercial enterprise that has been subjected to all kinds of examination and criticism, we should as regards government control go back on the fundamental doctrine of ministerial responsibility, I cannot understand. I believe the public will be infinitely more secure by holding the ministiy responsible for whatever is done and not restricting or freeing the ministry in its responsibility.

In view of the very strong feelings of my hon. friends, and in view, I think, of the fairness of the remarks made on all sides, I suggest that we let this subclause stand and, with the consent of the committee, take up subclause 2 of the same clause.

Hon. MAURICE DUPRE (Solicitor General) moved the second reading of and concurrence in an amendment made by the Senate to Bill No. 59, to amend the Penitentiary Act.
Penitentiary Act
What is the nature of the amendment?

By virtue of the Government Employees Compensation Act, any officer who is injured receives compensation. By virtue of Bill No. 59 he will also receive a gratuity, so in the case of an officer injured while handling a convict, for instance, he might receive a double gratuity, plus compensation. The object of the amendment is to ensure that an officer who is injured while handling a convict, for instance, will receive, not a double gratuity, but simply a gratuity plus compensation if he is eligible to compensation in virtue of provincial law.
Would the minister read the amendment if he has it available?

With pleasure. The amendment, which appears at page 412 of the votes and proceedings, reads as follows:
Subsection one of section thirty-two of the said act is further amended by adding thereto the following proviso:-
"Provided that the retiring allowance authorized by this subsection shall not be paid to any officer if he is eligible to receive compensation in respect of the infirmity or injury which has compelled his retirement from the service under and in virtue of the provisions of the Government Employees Compensation Act."
The idea is that he shall not receive two compensations at the one time?

Yes. But for this amendment he would receive double gratuity plus compensation. With this amendment he will receive simply his gratuity, plus compensation.
Mr. LaVERGNE: In this bill we seem to be legislating on a matter which is entirely provincial. The contract covering a man's services is a civil and provincial matter, and I do not know that this parliament has the power to legislate on a civil contract and determine questions of compensation, or how services shall be terminated, and under what conditions. A man may be dismissed for cause or without cause, and in our province the man may be open to receive compensation even if he is dismissed for cause, or even if his services were not definitely limited to a certain term. Under the French law, compensation has been awarded to a man who has lost his position although there was no fault either on his part or on the part of the company because a civil contract which has no term fixed is binding on the two parties and one

party cannot terminate it without paying compensation to the other party. We are here legislating on what I think is a civil matter.

Answering my hon. friend,
I do not think that we are in the least infringing upon provincial rights because by virtue of chapter 30 of the statutes of 1927, the Government Employees Compensation Act, any federal employee is entitled to the benefit of the provisions of any provincial act. At the present time there is a compensation act in every province, if I am not mistaken, therefore, the right to receive a pension is not taken away by the present measure. As heretofore the officer in charge will continue to receive compensation by virtue of the provincial legislation. All we enact is that in addition to that he will be entitled to receive a gratuity from the federal government. Any officer compelled to retire from the service on account of some mental or physical infirmity or injury will receive one gratuity. Any officer who has been hurt or injured by handling a convict or trying to prevent disturbances and so on, will receive double gratuity. We do not want a man who has been hurt while handling a convict or quelling a disturbance to be put on an inferior footing. If he is entitled to double gratuity he will not receive that double gratuity if he already receives compensation by virtue of provincial legislation. He will be entitled only to the gratuity, plus the compensation to which he is entitled by virtue of provincial legislation.
Mr. LaVERGNE:	What about the men
who are dismissed?
The house is not in committee. The hon. member may speak only once.

I understand that the only
right which is interfered with is the right created by the federal act. The amendment reads: "Provided the retiring allowance authorized by this subsection shall not be paid.." Mr. LaVERGNE:	What about employees
who are dismissed?

There is no interference with his provincial rights.

Hon. H. H. STEVENS (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved the second reading of Bill No. 79 to amend the Canada Grain Act.
Bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. LaVergne in the chair.
On section 1-Regulations.
I understand that the purpose of this bill is to carry out recommendations of the Board of Grain Commissioners?

I know the Prime Minister is a very hard worker but I should like to relate an instance which came to my notice. One of the officials of the Kiwanis club of the district of Washington wrote to the Secretary of State of the United States to ask if it would be possible to obtain a bottle of water from the House of Commons in Ottawa. There was a celebration to be held in Washington and the club wanted this water in order to drink a toast to Canada. The Secretary of State of the United States very gravely wrote to the Canadian minister in Washington to ask him if he could supply this sparkling fluid. The Canadian minister wrote to the Department of External Affairs, and I was just wondering if the department communicated with the office of the Prime Minister.
Oh yes.

If they did not communicate direct with the office of the Prime Minister, the subsequent actions were taken under the supervision of the Prime Minister himself. He gave instructions that his department should communicate with the Sergeant at Arms. The Sergeant at Arms gave instructions to the chief messenger to fill a clean bottle with water taken from a tap in the House of Commons. The chief messenger filled a bottle with water and returned it to the Sergeant at Arms. It was then turned over to the Department of External Affairs which sent it by special mail or express, I am not sure which-
Diplomatic courier.

The hon. member for Quebec South suggests that it probably went by diplomatic courier. However, the bottle was sent to the Secretary of State of the United States who forwarded it to the Canadian minister, who in turn had it conveyed to the president of the club.
It did not turn out to be anything else, did it?

This was during prohibition and probably the president of the Kiwanis club thought that there was something pleasant to the taste in the water drunk by the members of the House of Commons. The Prime Minister may be very busy with matters of state, but if his time is taken up with such things as sending a bottle of water from Ottawa to Washington, he might better stay here and listen to the speeches delivered by hon. members.

I am sorry the Prime Minister is not present as there was a matter I wanted to take up with him. However, as no other opportunity will be afforded, I will take up this matter under this item. On June 22, 1831, upon going into supply, I raised the question of the need of reopening the matter of compensation for the pelagic sealers on the Pacific coast. There was considerable debate at that time in which the Prime Minister took part at some length. He concluded with these words:
However, now that the opportunity presents itself I shall make inquiry and ascertain from a study of the documents whatever may be necessary to aid my somewhat fautly memory upon some of these points.
If that means anything, I take it to mean that he would look into the situation to see whether action was justified. It is quite a burning question out there. There are a number of people who feel they have been very hardly used in the matter. This is a complicated question with which I am not going to delay the committee now. There are three or four different classes of applicants who consider they have not received justice, and my suggestion was that the government should take into consideration the question whether they should not reopen the whole investigation. Judge Audette was sent out there a number of years ago. To prove that the matter is still a live one in the city of Victoria, I see by a newspaper paragraph that the city council is proposing to seek compensation under the pelagic sealing treaty for three old sealers who are now at the old men's home and it is proposed to ask the Dominion government to investigate the claims of the men, et cetera. It certainly is a question which, if there is any force in the argument that a thing is never settled until it is settled right, should be revived. As I say, I do not want to delay the committee by going into the merits of the matter, because it is too complicated, but I am strongly convinced and many men who are more conversant with the matter than I am are also convinced that certain classes of men are not getting a fair deal.

Supply-Miscellaneous
In regard to the tentative promise of the Prime Minister, I may say that I have been from time to time making attempts through his private secretary to find out whether anything has been done in the matter. I wrote to the private secretary first on December 27, 1931, again on May 10, 1932, again on August 25, 1932, and again on February 9, 1933. Not having received any reply, my only recourse is to bring the matter up in parliament. We are voting, I think, a substantial addition to some secretary's salary. I do not know whether it is this particular gentleman or not, but when a member writes to the secretary of the Prime Minister on a matter that has taken place in the house, he is entitled to a reply. On two occasions I did meet the gentleman and he told me orally that the matter was going to be dealt with or at any rate I would receive a reply, but that has not been forthcoming. I hope the Prime Minister will take notice of this and see that the matter is attended to. This is not a question as to whether I get an answer or not. I am quite indifferent to that. It is a question in respect to which a very substantial wrong has been done to a number of Canadian citizens. The money was appropriated to compensate them and they were not compensated. The money went into the consolidated revenue fund of Canada. I hope whoever is in charge for the moment of the item will bring this matter to the attention of the Prime Minister.
I shall certainly take steps to see that it is brought to his attention.

Item agreed to.
National Research Council, $404,500.

I want to make one observation on this vote. I am not criticizing the size of the vote, but I want to point out to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and to the Minister of Finance that in all the expressions which they have received from chambers of commerce all over Canada as to what might be done to reduce the expenditure of the administration not one has referred to this item.
I think that in this item lies the greatest opportunity for economy that might be practised by the government of Canada. I am informed that although the Dominion of Canada has built one of the finest research buildings to be found anywhere, with the definite intention of coordinating the research work of the various departments of government, there still remain thirty-four separate laboratories operating outside the research council building. I quite appreciate the difficulty that faces the Minister of Trade and Commerce, or whoever is the minister in charge of the estimates for the research council. I realize the desire of every deputy minister to retain within his department as many services as he can, and yet in these days when economy should be the watchword, and coordination of services should be resorted to in every way possible, it does seem to me a perfect disgrace that we should be main-
TSir George Perley.]
taining laboratories in so many different departments, and should not be coordinating the work of research when we have the facilities to do it.
I know perfectly well the attitude of the Prime Minister. I know that when he was leader of the opposition he felt at the time the research council was started that there would be difficulty in having the various departments release their research work so that it might all be coordinated. But I submit to the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce that there is no more effective way of practising economy at the present time than by compelling the deputy ministers who are retaining research departments of their own to help coordinate the work of research. These deputy ministers are all members of the research council, and there should be no rivalry. Research can be done better through coordination of effort in one building than by separate effort in scattered laboratories. Duplication would be avoided, and money would be saved. The research council building was erected for that purpose and I urge upon the Minister of Finance that he bring this matter to the attention of council, and that this duplication be done away with. The vote itself is not large enough. It is in the votes of other departments that savings could be effected.

I might in a word or two explain the situation. With much that the hon. member has said I am entirely in accord. The development or growth of these separate research laboratories in different departments is, I think, a matter for regret. We have had the matter under study for some time. Only a few weeks ago the Prime Minister and some of his colleagues were discussing the whole situation, and it is intended as soon as parliament prorogues to give the matter very careful study and do the utmost possible to coordinate these services.
Hear, hear.

There are a few of them that are necessary in other parts of the country; I Shall not go into detail, but coordination can be carried on under the direction and general aegis of the research council and its main central laboratories. .

I rise only to assure the minister that what he does in that regard will have the full cooperation of those who sit to the left of the Speaker; that was the very purpose for which these laboratories were built by the former government.

Publicity and advertising in Canada and abroad, including the sum of $100,000 for publicity and advertising in the United Kingdom and Europe to be administered by the High Commissioner for Canada, $173,500.

I have some
observations to make concerning the item for publicity and advertising in Canada and abroad, including the United Kingdom and Europe. This afternoon we passed rapidly a good many items. I should like to state that in passing those items we would not wish the committee to assume that we do not think there is room for a good deal more in the way of economy in regard to some expenditures of the departments. We realize, however, that at this stage of the session it is probably desirable to hasten matters along, and for that reason we have been content to refer only to one or two items which serve as illustrations of how further economies and avoidance of waste might be effected.
I have in my hand a full page advertisement which appeared in a great many Canadian newspapers. I shall ask the minister to tell the committee how many papers carried the advertisement, their names, and the amounts paid to each. The paper I hold in my hand is the Hamilton Spectator of Thursday, January 5, 1933. Before reading the advertisement I just wish to remind the house of what the Prime Minister himself said, namely, that in the last analysis, exports can be paid for only by imports. In that connection I should like the committee to keep in mind the effect of the government's restrictive tariff policies upon the possibility of extensive importations into Canada.
I believe this advertisement represents a waste of public money; money is simply being thrown away on this type of advertising. It cannot possibly bring in a return to any extent worthy of mention. The advertisement reads:
Canada expects that every producer, every business man, this year will do his duty. And under present conditions his supreme duty is

to export, as much as possible, whenever, wherever possible.
Canada never needed more export trade as urgently as she needs it to-day.
She needs it because of the employment it would provide for thousands of those who are now out of work.
She needs it because of the added production . it would give her with little or no increase in her overhead, thus improving her competitive position both at home and abroad.
She needs it because of the important part it would play in the solution of the international exchange problem.
Help to bring about a substantial increase in Canada's export trade, and better times will automatically follow.
New Opportunities Beckon
The new trade agreements now in effect with other parts of the British Empire create wonderful opportunities for increasing Canada's trade abroad. But to take full advantage of these new opportunities you must supply commodities which meet the requirements of overseas purchasers.
Price, quality, continuity of supply, these are the prime requisites in securing and maintaining overseas markets. Competition is keen. Purchasers are discriminating in their tastes and preferences. Study their needs and give them what they want, when they want it, and how they want it.
Help Canada by accepting Canada's offer to help you!
H. H. Stevens,
Minister of Trade and Commerce.
Mr. Chairman, that sort of lecture or exhortation to the commercial interests of Canada, paid for as advertising matter, is as good an example as could possibly be given of sheer waste of public money. What is needed for a furtherance of export trade is a change of policy on the part of hon. members opposite. Instead of telling Canadian exporters to do the impossible under conditions for which the government itself is largely responsible, let the government by its policies make it possible for the producers of this country to export. Will the minister explain the last sentence in the advertisement-"Give them what they want, when they want it, and how they want it"? What does that mean under present opportunities?

It means precisely what
it says. That is one of the things which is necessary more than anything else in Canada. The Canadian exporter must study the requirements of foreign markets, and must give them the articles they want in line as nearly as possible with their demands. He must study the markets abroad and time his exportations to suit the requirements of those markets. The right hon. gentleman has on several occasions, in fact ever since I took charge of this office, criticized me very bitterly

for anything that I have done at any time in connection with publicity. I am not desirous of entering into a lengthy discussion of the matter, but may I say briefly, that our exports, as far as quantity is concerned, leaving aside price, have been kept up remarkably well. I should like to make a suggestion. I understand that a charge is made of $2.50 for inspecting gas pumps. I had a complaint from Vancouver the other day. It is well known that some gasoline stations now have eight or ten different pumps, and the inspector comes along and charges the owner of the station $2.50 for every gasoline pump he has. I suggest that the minister take that under advisement, because it does not take long when the inspector is there to go over all the pumps. Many stations are complaining that it is too much to charge $2.50 for every pump they own.

I have already gone into the matter with care, and I cannot find that there are any hardships. The inspection is once a year. It is a protection to the seller of the gasoline as well as the public; particularly of course is it a protection to the public. It is a good service, well organized and carried on in an excellent manner, and while we have had a few complaints regarding

fees-very few-I have gone into that phase carefully and I see no reason to lower the fees. I can assure my hon. friend that the question has not been treated lightly.

May I call the minister's attention to the dissatisfaction that is prevalent concerning the manner in which coal is weighed. I think it has been brought to the minister's attention on several occasions within the last twelve months. The complaint is that the weighing of coal in the railway cars by the railway companies is not accurately done; very often the cars are short two, three or four tons. We think a more accurate method should be devised. Has the minister given the matter any consideration?

There may be isolated cases that I have not heard of. If the hon. gentleman has any information and would let me have it confidentially we will follow it up at once. But it must be apparent that there is a double check on this. The railways will weigh these cars to the maximum weight they hold for the purpose of getting the maximum revenue; for the charge is according to weight. There may be occasional inaccuracies, but they are rare. I think the business is now on a very excellent basis. But I shall be glad to have any information of that character, and to look into it at once.
I think information was sent to the minister some twelve months ago.

Mail subsidies and steamship subventions- Atlantic ocean-Pacific ocean-local services, $2,172,930.

There is a very large
increase in the Canada-United Kingdom and Canada-South Africa services, also in the Pacific service, Canada-China and Japan, over what was granted a few years ago. I wish the minister would explain those increases.

The increases arise out of this situation; the steamship lines of competing countries are subsidized very heavily, to the extent of at least three times what we are paying. Our steamship service in these waters is of vital interest to the maintenance of our trade routes. The matter was very carefully considered, and we decided that in order to keep these splendid mail, passenger

and freight services going it was absolutely essential that very substantial subsidies should be granted, and as my hon. friend knows these subsidies were adopted two or three years ago.
Then with regard to the item for South Africa, there is a splendid opportunity at the present time for an expansion of our trade from the Pacific coast with South Africa, touching also the easterly coast of that country. While that service has not been allocated or tenders called for, later on it is intended to have that done. The object is to establish a continuity of service on the Pacific between Canada and South Africa. At present our goods are carried there by lines operating directly from San Francisco and Seattle. Briefly this is the explanation for these two items.

I have no objection to
the old-established subsidy with regard to the service on the Atlantic between Canada and South Africa, nor have I any objection to the new service which the minister proposes to establish between Canada and South Africa on the Pacific. This subsidy for service between Canada, 'China and Japan, however, is a very large item, and I should like to know to whom it is paid.
The Canadian Pacific.

I submit to the minister that this is another case of an abnormally large subsidy being paid to encourage trade, While the purpose is defeated by one of his own colleagues. Some time ago I pointed out to the Minister of National Revenue that raw silk could be imported into New York without the application of any dumping duty at all, whereas in Canada the Customs department applied a currency valuation which allows a dumping duty on this article. A man buying a hundred thousand yen worth of silk, which would be about $25,000 worth, could save $1,400 by buying that silk in New York instead of buying it in Tokyo and importing it by Canadian steamships through a Canadian port. Here we have the Minister of National Revenue making it easier for the silk to be taken via the Panama canal to New York than to be brought directly to Vancouver, and yet in the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce we have this very substantial sum of $659,000 being voted which is paid the Canadian Pacific in order to encourage trade with Japan. I submit to the minister that this is a very large subsidy. Some years ago the British government wanted to secure the flagship of the Atlantic, and subsidized the Cunard line to

construct the Lusitania and the Mauritania. The subsidy granted amounted to S364,000 per year per ship. The British government got two fast transatlantic transports, which they could and did use for troop ships in time of war; they had the flagship of the Atlantic, and all this for a sum not much greater than the amount we here ask for one service. In my opinion $659,000 is a very substantial amount, and is quite out of line with the volume of tonnage being carried on the route. I believe this first item of $535,000 to subsidize the line between Canada and the United Kingdom on the Atlantic is justifiable to some extent because it includes the farmer subsidies for mail service.
The Pacific subsidy includes mail service also.

But these two items, totalling practically $1,200,000 a year, at 5 per cent would represent a capital investment of $24,000,000. In consideration of the volume of trade that is moving at present I consider them very generous subsidies.
My hon. friend has not been quite fair in his analysis. Previously we paid the cost of carrying the mails, but that is included in this service.
How much was that?

I was looking for that information, but I do not seem to have it here. It is a very substantial amount. On the Canada-Australia service the cost of carrying the mail is greater than the subsidy we give, and we may have to bring that back to where it was formerly in the supplementary estimates. Then there is another point: On the Pacific coast the United States pay a subsidy of $5,000,000 for the China-Japan service.
But they have a large volume of business.

We have a very substantial business also with both China and Japan, and our trade with those countries is increasing. On the Atlantic these subsidies ensure a service which could not be maintained otherwise, at least in these days. We thus provide for the carrying of the mails and we have a fast, all-Canadian route. My conviction, after going into the matter with great care, is that we are justified in paying these subsidies.
Has the minister any figures that would indicate the percentage of the total trade passing over this route which would be represented by this subsidy?

No, I do not think so; the figures never have been segregated in. that way. There is no question as to the remarkably fine service given by this company with regard to high class freight going from Canada to the orient. Our high class package freight moves with very great dispatch.
But the volume is small.
It is very considerable.

Yes.

Yes.

The committee will remember that last year I discussed the matter of the employment of orientals on subsidized Canadian ships. At that time I pointed out that while it was true that we had no control over the employment of seamen on ships operated by private owners, we as a country should give a lead in seeing that something is done to have more Canadians employed at least on our subsidized ships. At the present time there are 2,573 orientals engaged on ships running out of the Pacific coast while over 2,000 white seamen are without employment.

Where do those ships ply
to?

The Canadian Pacific Steamships Limited operates a line between Vancouver and the orient. The steamship Empress of Asia employs 500 orientals; the Empress of Canada employs 500; the Empress of Japan, 495, and the Empress of Russia, 500, while each ship has a personnel, including the captain and engineer, of only 60 to

65 white Canadian seamen. In the coastwise service, 107 orientals are employed by the Canadian Pacific Steamships Limited while the Union Steamships Limited employs 90. Large subsidies are paid to these companies. I believe I am correct in stating that a subsidy of $4,950 per outward trip per ship is paid to the British Canadian Steamships Limited which employs approximately 300 orientals.
Does Japan pay any subsidies to these companies?

My information is that they
do not. I understand, and the minister can correct me if I am wrong, that this company sometimes charter other ships, and that they receive the same subsidy for each outward journey, and this is money which they obtain for very little outlay. After investigating this matter, I have come to the conclusion that these subsidies do not help the lumbering industry of British Columbia. I think it was last year that the minister pointed out that they were given in order to encourage this industry, but I do not think they help at all.

Will the hon.
gentleman please explain himself a little further?
You might object to the former Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) who started these.

If they were given to companies employing orientals I would have taken exactly the stand I am taking right now. I understand that a Mr. MacMillan is in charge of lumber sales for British Columbia. When he receives an order the rates are quoted to various parts of the world, to China, to Australia, to New Zealand or some other country. I maintain that the lumber would be shipped just as cheaply to these particular countries even though no subsidies were paid. At the present moment ships come to the Fraser river to load lumber for Great Britain and other parts of the world. Although they are not subsidized by their respective governments, they carry the lumber at as reasonable rates as this subsidized company.
I think it is about time that we in Canada began to look after our own people a little bit. Every other country is giving encouragement to the employment of its own nationals as seamen.' When a Norwegian ship comes to Vancouver or New Westminster it is manned by Norwegian seamen; British ships are manned by British seamen, the Australian 
ships by Australian seamen, but when it comes to our own ships, no encouragement whatever is given to the employment of Canadian seamen. When subsidies are paid by the people of Canada, Canadian seamen should be employed. There is another- matter to which I would like to refer but it is one for Which perhaps the Minister of Trade and Commerce has no responsibility. Ships of British registry entering the ports of British Columbia will not engage Canadian seamen. I should like to read a sworn statement by one Paul Bailey. It reads:
He says regarding his application for a position on the steamship Janeta, which I believe is a British vessel:
That I produced my discharge certificate numbered 10094 as aforesaid, and opened the same showing the entries covering my periods of employment from the year 1925 to date.
That after perusing the same, the said master informed me that I could not obtain employment unless I had a British Board of Trade discharge book, and was domiciled in England.
That I was born in Canada and have always lived in Canada, and I explained this to the master, but he still refused to give me employment for the reasons aforesaid.
That the assistant shipping master who was present did not inform the master of the vessel that Canadian born seamen who have resided in Canada are unable to obtain British board certificates in Canada, and that my certificate of discharge book is the proper certificate for me to have, and is the certificate that is generally accepted, at the port of Vancouver by British masters seeking to employ firemen or trimmers.
That I am informed and verily believe that the said ss. Janeta-
That is the ship the master of which refused to hire this Canadian seaman because he was not domiciled in England and did not have a British board of trade certificate.
-is subsidized by the Canadian government, and that the said vessel is trading between Canada and the orient and that I am advised and verily believe that the refusal of the said master to employ me. by reason of my failure to possess a British Board of Trade certificate was improper.
That suitable regulations covering cases of this kind should be forthwith made to prevent repetition of these occurrences affecting myself and other seamen.
And I solemnly make this declaration conscientiously believing the same to be true and knowing it to be of the same force and effect as if made under oath and by virtue of the Canada Evidence Act.
He signed this before a justice of the peace. It was sent to me by the Canadian Seamen's Institute of Vancouver, along with one or two other affidavits to the effect that Canadian seamen could not obtain employment on British ships coming to the ports of New Westminster and Vancouver.

Supply-Trade-Subsidies
It is high time that we in this country take serious note of the fact that no encouragement whatever is given to our seamen and young men to follow the calling of the sea. It is annoying to think we would have that number of orientals employed on ships on the Pacific trading between foreign ports or carrying on coastwise trade, when there are in the ports of New Westminster and Vancouver more than 3,000 Canadian seamen who are willing to work and who are just as competent as, if not more competent than, the orientals, but who cannot obtain positions or employment on those ships on account of the fact that orientals are given the preference.
It has been stated before that if we commenced to curtail the employment of orientals, Japan or some other foreign country might take note of the fact. It might be interesting to the committee to know that Australia, which has gone very far in that sort of legislation and which does not allow ships with oriental crews to unload in her ports, a move which one might consider very drastic, has been doing far more trade during the past three or four years with Japan and China than Canada has. But I come back to the point that every country is giving encouragement to its own nationals while we in Canada ignore this entirely, although we have on the entrance to the parliament buildings the words:
The wholesome sea is at her gates,
Her gates both east and west.

North should have
been added to that.

I am willing to add that, only I hope when the north is added, the unwholesome conditions that we have on the Pacific coast will not be found there also.
The situation in the east is different from that on the Pacific, because ships from eastern Canadian ports are employing Canadians.
Mr. LaVERGNE: No.

Two days ago the question was asked in the railway committee and I was informed that boats belonging to the Canadian National and plying between Atlantic ports and the West Indies were employing Canadian citizens. If that is the case, I am pleased to hear it.
Mr. LaVERGNE: They are not.
That was my information. I am sorry to hear they are not. That makes the situation all the worse.

Whom are they employing?
Mr. LaVERGNE: Englishmen, Scotchmen or Welshmen, but not Canadians.

It has been stated that many of these orientals are British subjects, and I believe if they come from some Chinese ports, they claim to be British subjects, but no one can be sure *yvhether they are or not. Personally I doubt their statements. But what I want is that we employ our own people, because the Asiatic, whether he calls himself or actually is a British subject, is of a nonassimilable race. I could point out the danger that might arise, if war broke out in the Pacific, with all these orientals on board these ships. Take, for example, ships with a crew of 600 orientals and only a few whites. It may be said that orientals are necessary in carrying oriental passengers. We are not objecting to a few orientals being carried on these ships, but we are objecting to the employment of hundreds of orientals as against a very few whites. I urge upon the minister and the committee that we show the way to the others by inserting in the contracts for our subsidized lines some provision that on a mail subsidized ship or one subsidized for the carrying of cargo, greater consideration be given to our own Canadian citizens.

Just'a brief reply to my hon. friend. In the first place it must be borne in mind that these ships are running from a Canadian port to two oriental countries, China and Japan, and in the question of international trade one must respect the rights of one country just as much as those of another.
In regard to the Canadian Pacific ships which make Hongkong their terminal port in China and Vancouver their terminal port on this side, as the hon. gentleman has pointed out many of the crews are British subjects taken on at Hongkong. I tei him very candidly now as I told the house last year, that we certainly cannot suggest a discrimination agaist British subjects from any part of the British Empire, whatever their race, colour or creed may be.
My hon. friend says that the British-Can-adian steamship service is of no use to British Columbia.
I said to the lumber industry.
I was going to say that he had better address that observation to the lumber interests of British Columbia.
I certainly shall.

As a matter of fact, it has been of very great assistance to the lumber trade of British Columbia, particularly in the
Supply-T rade-Subsidies

last year or so. This service was started several years ago. The first contract was with Mr. H. R. MacMillan, who, if not a shipowner, was a ship charterer and carried on his business in that way. He had a three year contract entered into with my predecessor in office. At that time he ran to Australia, but the last two years or thereabouts he ran to China. I have before me the figure as to the lumber carried and it runs into a very considerable amount. The main reason for the granting of that subsidy was to assist in the moving of lumber freely from British Columbia. It was considered to have been a good service and profitable to that province in its results. Last June or thereabouts this contract ran out and we called for tenders for another one. While under the previous contract we paid $7,700 a trip, the British Canadian Steamship Company made a tender at $4,950 a trip, a very greatly reduced amount, and they were given the business. They have two ships not only wholly Canadian owned but built in the city of Vancouver during the latter part of the war by the Coughlan shipyard, and those ships have been operated by them ever since. In addition to those two ships, on one or two occasions they have had additional lumber offering to what they were able to carry and they asked for the privilege of an extra voyage; they chartered a ship and they got that privilege. I would not stand in their way and they moved the lumber and moved it quickly. These chartered ships in practically every instance were British bottoms. Obviously it would be unwise for this government to dictate to the shipping interests of Canada or Great Britain just what type of crew they should carry.
I can tell the committee frankly that we have gone into this matter with considerable care, and there is no way, apart from abandoning the contract altogether, in which we could dictate to them what crews they should carry. It is true we could put in a clause that they must carry only Canadian crews. That could be done, but the service would cost a tremendous amount more. I am not desirous of entering into any argument or discussion over this matter; I am merely stating the facts as they exist. Take, for instance, the Canadian Pacific boats. A very large proportion of their passengers carried in the second class and in the steerage are orientals, and it is quite obvious, without desiring to make any invidious comparisons, that white crews would not serve oriental passengers of the steerage and second class on board those ships. That is the experience of these fMr. Stevens.]
shipping concerns in oriental waters. Besides, there is an element of fairness in this, because we are seeking to develop trade between Canada and China and Japan, and I think it would ill become Canada through its parliament to discriminate against the citizens of the countries with which we are seeking to develop trade. There is an element of fairness and common sense in this case which must be recognized.
The hon. gentleman also stated that the trade was no good for Canada. I happen to have under my hand a letter dated March 6 last which I shall quote in part to indicate the value of this British-Canadian Steamship Service in carrying lumber freight from the province of British Columbia to the orient. It is addressed to myself by Mr. Day of the Federal Lumber Company, and reads in part:
When you appointed the Ocean Shipping Company Limited of Vancouver, B.C., to receive the subsidy to China, we were greatly encouraged, as this is solely a shipping company. Mr. E. S. Day, president of the Federal Lumber Company. We have abundance of evidence that this service is highly appreciated by the lumber interests of British Columbia. I may tell the committee very frankly that I am not prepared at this time to say that we should attempt to dictate to the steamship companies the ratings that they should carry on their ships. This is a matter that has been well worked out among the shipping interests of the world. We do endeavour to limit the vessels to British ships when British ships are available. It is true that in previous years Swedish or Norwegian ships have occasionally been chartered, but not many. The ships were largely British bottoms chartered by MacMillan, who held the previous three-year contract, and by the present contractors. There are two British Columbia built boats, and one or two other ships which were British bottoms have been chartered; That is virtually all there is to say on the matter, Mr. Chairman. Personally I

amount, but I know one dollar a cubic foot was paid.
