to have that information.

I should like to say one or two words more before the item passes. I cannot agree with the minister when he states that we in Canada cannot dictate who shall be employed on subsidized ships. It seems strange that Canada should take the stand that she cannot do it when other countries of no greater importance do it. Yet we seem to be afraid; the minister says that it would interfere with trade and that any interference would be dangerous to Canada. We know that no ships carrying oriental crews can unload in Australia ; yet Australia has prospered as much as Canada. Before the depreciation of the yen and the general depreciation in exchange currencies, in the years 1928,1929,1930 and 1931, she did more business than Canada did with Japan and China, yet Australia excludes the Oriental entirely. They have a law under which they allow no Chinamen or Japanese into their country. Despite those facts their trade has not been harmed. From the Canadian Association of Seamen I have a letter, part of which is as follows:
Our investigation committee discovered that Italian ships, Norwegian, Swedish or Danish, German, French, Chinese and Japanese all

carried their own nationals aboard their ships, but when it came to the examination of vessels flying the British flag and sailing under Canadian registry, to our amazement they reported that there were 2,573 orientals on Canadian registered vessels, and on rechecking these figures wo discovered that number if anything was a conservative estimate.
I cannot agree with -the minister when he states that we cannot dictate, and I believe it is about time we did dictate, on behalf of our own people, and especially when we -are paying over a million dollars in subsidies to ships and plying on the Pacific out of New Westminster or Vancouver. The item before us is for $995,540, and I think that figure is further augmented by a subsidy of $4,950 per month. Before I sit down I should like to ask if the Empress liners are being overhauled at Esquimalt dock. Last year some arrangements were made I believe for overhauling in Esquimalt and I believe the Canadian Pacific did consider overhauling at that point. Are they having their ships overhauled at Esquimalt?

Generally speaking they
have been overhauling at Hongkong; I believe -that has been the practice for about thirty years. One ship was overhauled at Esquimalt last year.

Yo-u gave way on some of
th-e docking charges.

The largest dock in Canada
is situated at Esquimalt; it could take care of -the largest liner. Yet this company, receiving so much money from the people of Canada and flying a Canadian or British flag, according to -the point of registration-because some of the ships are registered in London, England, and some in Canada-and carrying oriental crews, are not willing to spend any money in Canada; when they want any overhauling done they go to Hongkong and leave our own yards idle. I object very much to the Canadian Pacific or any other company using oriental crews and having their work done at other points, especially when that company is subsidized and assisted by Canadian funds.

I should like to consolidate as briefly as I can my criticism of two items in the estimates. The people of Canada are asked to vote $659,000 for service between Canada and China and Japan, a

Supply-Trade-Subsidies
vote which did not exist in the year 1930 when this government came into power. They are also being asked to vote subsidies between Canada and the United Kingdom on the Atlantic for $535,000, another vote which did not exist in 1930 when this government took office.
The minister points out that part of this service is the carriage of mail. In the estimates for the Post Office Department for the year 1930, at page 73, we find that the total amount of money paid by the Post Office Department of the Dominion of Canada for the carriage of mail by steamship, on all services, Atlantic, Pacific and internal, amounted to only $530,000. Therefore, if we allowed all the money which the Post Office Department paid for these two services we find that we still have an increase on these two services alone of well on to $700,000. I submit to the minister that the trade of Canada at the present time does not justify any such increase in the amounts paid to steamship companies. In 1928 our trade with Japan was $32,000,000 export and $12,000,000 import, and no subsidy of $659,000 was paid to carry that trade. True the American government do give subsidies, but they give a less rate per capita or per ton of freight than Canada. This trade would move without any such substantial subsidy.
As to the other items in the estimates, I have very little complaint. I believe they are the ordinary subsidies which have been granted for many years. The subsidies to New Zealand and Australia are quite in line with the volume of business carried; they amount to only $60,000 or $70,000. But these other amounts are very substantial. One of these subsidies is as large as the British government paid for the building of the Mauretania and the Lusitania, the two ships of the Cunard line which gave Great Britain the blue ribbon of the Atlantic, and two of the finest troopships for use in time of emergency. I submit that the minister should reduce these estimates.
How long has this $659,000 item been in the estimates?
This is the third year.

May I
in a word support what has been said by the hon. member for North Bruce and the hon. member for New Westminster. The minister rather suggested, although he was not very definite, that the company which is getting this tremendous subsidy could not compete if it employed none but white seamen. He also suggested, I gather, that international
complications might result from excluding from employment on ships in this trade the subjects of other nations across the Pacific.
I suggest that that argument does not apply. Especially in a service subsidized by the Canadian government we should insist that at least a substantial majority, say seventy-five per cent, of all ranks on the ships should be Canadian seamen. The minister knows as well as I do that the feeling on the Pacific coast, especially in Vancouver and New Westminster, in regard to this matter is becoming very acute. I suggest that in a time of unemployment and emergency over 3,000 of our Canadian unemployed in these ports, men well qualified for all grades of service, could be given work on these ships. When we are giving such a tremendous subsidy to one company it should be on the condition that at least a substantial majority of those employed should be our own Canadian seamen.
I agree with the hon. member for North Bruce in regard to the major portion of the 84 subsidies; I think they serve a good purpose and help to develop the trade of the Pacific coast, but I am sure the minister himself would like to see our Canadian seamen employed. The day will soon come when we must insist on this or cease paying the subsidy. It would be of tremendous help in solving our unemployment problem; it would remove two or three thousand unemployed from the coast cities of British Columbia, and the same thing might apply on the Atlantic. Now that Canada has assumed all the obligations of nationhood, I do not see why we should not restrict this employment to our own sailors, to the exclusion of others, including those of other countries of the empire. I think our own men are as well qualified as any, possibly not as engineers, but in most grades of service. I think an administration elected on the cry of "Canada first" should carry that policy to its logical conclusion and restrict employment on lines subsidized or controlled by Canada to Canadian seamen.

I was very interested in what
the hon. member for North Bruce said in reference to the difference between the amount of trade done from Pacific coast ports to China and Japan this year and last compared with the trade done three or four years ago. There is no doubt about that.

It is due entirely to the policies of this government. The foreign trade of this country has decreased more than fifty per cent. In 1929-30 the trade was $2,600,000,000, but due to the policies of this government it has decreased until now it is only something like $800,000,000.
All the fault of the government!

And the hon. member for
Stanstead (Mr. Hackett)! The reason the government is compelled to pay these larger subsidies is that if the subsidies were not increased these steamers could not continue to operate on the small amount of cargo which is now being carried.
I notice that the minister has been rather generous to 'his own province. Of course he represents a constituency in British Columbia, yet he is Minister of Trade and Commerce for the whole of Canada. I am not going to object at the moment to the fact that a very large part of the several subsidies under the heading of the Pacific coast is paid in order to encourage the export of lumber from British Columbia ports. If the minister in his capacity as Minister of Trade and Commerce thinks it is in the interest of Canada that subsidies should be granted for the carriage of lumber from Pacific coast ports, then I say that as Minister of Trade and Commerce for the whole of Canada he should also have provided that the same treatment be given to the ports on the Atlantic ocean. We on the Atlantic coast are just as much entitled to have ships subsidized and encouragement given as they are in the province of British Columbia. Perhaps after I sit down the minister will give the committee reasons why he has picked out one province and ignored the Atlantic ports, because as far as the lumber industry is concerned that is what he has done; there is no money voted in these estimates to encourage the lumber trade from Atlantic ports.
There is another matter to which I want to refer. I notice that while the minister has been giving these large subsidies to British Columbia, and has voted a new item of $100,000 for one service alone, in respect to the small local services in the maritime provinces, he has not only reduced the amounts previously paid but has cut several of them out altogether. There is a very important service between the city of Saint John, New Brunswick, and the town of Digby, Nova Scotia. It is not only a convenient service to local travellers between those ports, but also to passengers travelling between Mont-
real and Nova Scotia using the bay of Fundy route. Yet I notice that the minister proposes, in order to provide this $100,000 for the shipping interests in British Columbia, to cut out entirely the subsidy given for the steamship service between Saint John and Digby. Hon. ALFRED iDURANLEAU (Minister of Marine): I have been deeply interested in the observations of the hon. member concerning the harbour of New Westminster. When this item was called the other day I was speaking to it when six o'clock was called. I was referring to the oriental problem. I would point out that it is really getting very serious, especially with the fishermen on the Fraser river. The Japanese are practically getting control there. Last spring, although the cannery men had certain boats of their own operating on the Fraser river, the Japanese told the cannery men just how many fish they would get each morning and also dictated the terms to them. I have that on the best authority, that of two cannery men on the Fraser river. My own observation is that the issuing of licences to Japanese is practically allowing the Japanese to build up a part of Japan on the Canadian Pacific coast. It is a well known fact that many of the Japanese who obtained fishing licences were naval officers and were here acquiring knowledge of the British Columbia coast before going back to their country with the knowledge thus acquired. That is generally recognized and well known. They were spying, really, and I am not afraid to say so. Another point, Mr. Chairman, is that when licences are issued to white fishermen they cannot swap them around, so to speak, as the Japanese do, because the Japanese are not so easily recognized as are the white men. Last year I complained to the department in Vancouver that the Japanese boats fished during the whole twenty-four hours; there are two and sometimes three different crews on each boat. If that were attempted by the white fishermen they would be jacked up and a charge laid against them or the licence cancelled, but the Japanese can carry on that practice. They have one licence to a boat, but they simply pass the licence from one to another and once the boats get out they stay out, while other boats come around and collect the fish. I went into this matter rather exhaustively the other day, but since I had no reply from the minister I rose on this occasion to ask if he would take this matter into very serious consideration. The New Westminster Fishermen's Protective Association went on record unanimously in this regard; I attended a meeting where about one hundred fishermen took a standing vote asking that the licences to Japanese be reduced. They realize how serious this question is becoming, especially on the Fraser river where so many Japanese are operating, and where in large measure they are obtaining control of the industry. Last year when orders were received from Japan for salted and smoked fish, which were plentiful at the time, no orders were given the white fishermen; they were all spread around among their own nationals. I should like to ask the minister if he will give this matter serious consideration with a view of curtailing the number of these licences by at least ten per cent each year. This was proposed a few years ago, but it was discontinued because the courts at that time declared that we had no power to do so. Since then, however, the statute of Westminster has been passed and I believe we have now all the power necessary to prohibit anyone we may desire from securing a licence.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: We shall be very glad to look into the matter, Mr. Chairman. I know the reduction of licences to Japanese was suspended for two or three years because the matter was before the courts, but if we have a free hand now we will see that the number of licences is reduced. As to the use of forged naturalization papers, my hon. friend is well aware that my department has done everything possible to stop that practice by having inspectors follow the operations of these fishermen and prosecute everyone caught using false papers. As a matter of fact I am told that this practice has ceased.
Not entirely.

Practically.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I shall be glad to
have my officials on the western coast have an eye on what is going on there, and we will prosecute everyone who is found to be breaking the law.

There is another serious matter with regard to fish; I refer to the embargo on sockeye salmon, which prohibits fishermen from exporting the raw fish. This embargo was put on at the instigation of the eanners, who complained that if the British Columbia fishermen were allowed to sell their fish in the best market it might curtail the activities of the eanners. That was the argument advanced by the canneries association to the minister and his deputy in favour of this embargo. I do not know of any other branch of industry that is prohibited from selling its products in the best market available. Up to last year the United States fishermen were receiving from 15 cents to 35 cents more for each salmon than was being paid in British Columbia. Last year, however, the prices across the line dropped for some reason, and what did the eanners do? They immediately forsook the white fishermen and went across the line to purchase salmon; at one time they brought in 27,000 sockeye salmon from Puget sound. It was all very well for the eanners to say, "We will not allow you fishermen to sell across the line," but when it suited them they practically told the fishermen to do whatever they liked with their fish because they could buy salmon across the line for less. The British Columbia Packers, Limited, the Canadian Fishing Company, Limited, the Colonial Packers, Limited and two other firms, I understand, went across the line to purchase large quantities of salmon because they could get them for a little less. In view of this I appeal to the minister to have the embargo lifted entirely in order to allow the fishermen to sell their fish wherever they like. Can you imagine the situation that would be created if a farmer who had wheat or potatoes to sell should be told that he could not sell those products in the best market? A fisherman buys a boat and a net, but when he brings in the fish he is told that he cannot take sockeye salmon out of the country. He cannot ship it fresh, although as I say in past years the fishermen across the line received from 15 cents to 35 cents per fish more than the Canadian fishermen received. In view of the fact that the eanners broke their own bargain, so to speak, and last year purchased- large quantities of salmon in the United States, I ask the minister to lift this embargo.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Now that my hon.
friend has brought this matter to my attention it will be seriously considered.

For a few moments I should
like to bring up a matter that was discussed at some length previously; I refer to order in council 206, but to-night I will approach this question from another angle. With all due respect to the legal ability of the minister and his associates I submit that this order in council is ultra vires; there is no question about it. It is rotten with regard to the question of fairness and equity, and apparently it is equally rotten in law. Section 92 of the British North America Act sets out the jurisdiction of the dominion and provincial governments respectively, and subsection 13 states that all matters pertaining to property and civil rights shall come within the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces. Of course there is a way in which that can be evaded in a sense; I think it was done by the former Minister of Agriculture, under somewhat similar circumstances, with regard to the grading of eggs. He got the provincial governments to pass what is called concurrent legislation. The minister got the government of British Columbia to do something similar in connection with these regulations, and on April 13 of last year they passed chapter IV of the statutes of British Columbia, 1932, which was a bill containing three sections. Section 1 made valid any act or regulations made thereunder passed by the Dominion government before that date. The original inspection regulations were passed on April 4 of last year, I think, so they just came within 'the scope of that section. Section 2, however, sets out what is to happen in future, that is, as from April 13, 1932; it states very plainly and simply-I need not read the section-that any other regulations passed by the Dominion government will not be valid in British Columbia unless proclaimed by the lieutenant-governor in council. This order in council 206, bad cess to it, has not been so proclaimed, and the dhances are a thousand to one against its being proclaimed, because the British Columbia legislature unanimously passed a resolution emphatically objecting to it, so I very much doiibt if the government would have the courage-or perhaps the gall-to proclaim it now. That being the case, where does this government get authority to come into British Columbia and interfere with the property and civil rights of the people of that province? If I catch fish, I must do it under dominion

Supply-Fisheries
jurisdiction because they have control over the fisheries, but under the decision of the privy council made several years ago, once the fish were caught they come under the jurisdiction of the province. We amended the fisheries act last year in order to have it accord with those views. Once the fish are caught, they come under the jurisdiction of the province and the dominion can exercise no control. But they now come along and say that they are going to have control. I know the argument that will be used; it will be said that the dominion has control as far as exports are concerned. There is no doubt the dominion can make regulations to deal with the packaging, the marketing or branding of anything to be exported, but I do not think the dominion should attempt to go beyond that and wrest jurisdiction away from a province. Subsection 26a of the original inspection regulation states that "all salmon shall be inspected." It is not salmon that is to be exported, or this or that, but all salmon. That is amplified in subsequent subsections which state where it shall be inspected. When a shipment of canned salmon is destined outside of Canada, it must be inspected at a certain place, and if it is destined inside of Canada, it must be inspected at another place. I ask the committee to note the words "inside of Canada." The argument of interprovincial trade cannot be used, because that clause would cover salmon to be shipped from one part of the province to another. That is provincial trade and I claim that any dominion legislation which attempts to interfere with such trade is ultra vires.
It may be said: We will exercise our jurisdiction as far as we can on export stuff and leave out the provincial trade. Ordinary regulations to cover branding, packing and so forth would be reasonable enough, but this order in council 206 begins to operate before the fish are caught, or at least immediately after. It states that the fish must be landed at the cannery wharf within twenty-four hours after being caught. Let me give a definite illustration. Suppose I catch some salmon according to the laws of British Columbia. I go ahead and can them and ignore order in council 206. I claim I am operating in British Columbia and I have nothing to do with that order in council. Having got my salmon canned, a situation arises where I find it desirable to export them. What can I do with them? I cannot do anything with them; I cannot sell them in British Columbia and I cannot export them. I would have to go back and take them out of the cans and deliver them at the wharf twenty-four hours after being caught. That
is not a condition subsequent to inspection or subsequent to the determination to export, it is a condition antecedent. Whether or not I am going to export my salmon, even though I intend to sell them within the province, I will be compelled to can the salmon in accordance with this order in council. That would be depriving me of my right to carry on my business according to the laws of British Columbia, and it would be depriving the province of its jurisdiction. It might be said: You could sell your salmon to a broker. But no broker would have anything to do with them because he would not be able to export them if needed. I am advised by able lawyers that this is ultra vires. If the government attempts to enforce it it will be laying itself open to litigation.
There is another point I intend to bring up, but before I do so I should like the minister to make a reply. I have no doubt this matter has been engaging the attention of his officials.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I have listened with
much interest to the argument of my hon. friend as to the legality of order in council 206. Let me say to him, however, that no action was taken without first submitting the whole thing to the Department of Justice. As a matter of fact, the order in council was drafted by the officials of that department. I would not think of having such an order in council prepared without the advice of the Department of Justice. My hon. friend may be quite correct in his statement of the law, but my duty is to rely upon the advice of the Department of Justice.
As far as the question of the proclamation of the regulation by the provincial authorities is concerned, I may say that a request was sent some time ago to the provincial government asking that this be done. I cannot say that it has been done up to date. My hon. friend says that it will not be done because the legislature has unanimously repudiated the regulation. As yet we have had no report from the Premier of British Columbia but I hope that if the department insists upon this regulation being put into force, the provincial authorities will issue the necessary proclamation. If they do not do so, it will apply to goods to be exported.

The minister says that the
order in council was drawn by the Department of Justice. I have no doubt that they were cognizant of the British Columbia legislation and that they naturally assumed that a proclamation would be issued in the ordinary course of events. However, the fact is that
Supply-Fisheries

there is now every possibility of its not being proclaimed. The question then arises whether this government has the right under this excuse-it is nothing more than an excuse-* of helping the export trade to compel that the same method be adopted with fish to be sold within the province. The minister says that he hopes the provincial government will proclaim the regulation, but I most sincerely hope that they will not. I doubt very much if it would be legal to do it. Surely the whole legislature is superior to the cabinet, and that legislature passed the resolution which I read the other night stating that they emphatically protested against the resolution. I cannot conceive of any government with a sense of its responsibility acting in defiance of the unanimous wish of the legislature. However, some weird things have been done by the present government of British Columbia and it is just possible that they will take that action.
If they do not proclaim the regulation, I think the government would be well advised to drop the whole matter. I am sure it will prove utterly unworkable and will offer every opportunity for litigation. The government has no right to insist that all canned salmon must be inpected without having concurrent provincial legislation. If they had said, "all canned salmon destined for export," it would have been a different thing, but we are dealing with the regulation as it now stands. It is so easy to start litigation and so difficult to snd it, with all the cost that is involved. Why not ask for a reference to the supreme jourt and get a ruling on the matter before die government upsets the whole industry and jets into serious trouble through litigation?
There is another objection I should like to point out. The minister says that the Department of Justice drew up this order in council. Well, perhaps a lawyer did so, but I do not think it was somebody familiar with the fishing industry of British Columbia. It will be noticed that the order in council was passed on February 3. There are two objections to it. The first is that the government passed it on February 3, and although this is almost the end of April, the government has not yet put into effect the method by which it may be ascertained whether those fish were caught within twenty-four hours before being canned. The minister says that somebody is to take an oath. But that is not specified by the order in council and it is not in effect until this is done. This half-baked order in council had been put into force and it will

be necessary to pass another order in council to make it effective. This order in council was passed on February 3 and I suppose anyone will agree that it took effect when it was passed. Consequently on February 3, the law was that all canned salmon thereafter examined that are found by the board of inspection to be so-and-so shall get a certificate, but provided that no such certificate shall be issued for canned salmon that had not been landed fresh at a cannery for canning twenty-four hours after being caught. That is in force now; that is the law. If to-morrow I take 10,000 cases to be inspected, I have to prove that last June or July the salmon were landed on a wharf twenty-four hours after being caught. This order in council came into effect on February 3, 1933. Canning begins some time in June and lasts until about the end of October, and I think I am safe in saying that not half of the canners can get their fish inspected by February 3. The matter of course depends upon t'he season. A year or two ago-and the deputy minister can corroborate me-in the month of June, right at the beginning of the next season there were 450,000 cases of one variety of salmon on hand. We have evidence of that. That might have been an exceptional pack, but that was only one variety. I have, however, no hesitation in saying that on February 3 the larger portion of the salman pack of 1932 was on hand and had not been inspected. Therefore it was subject to P.C. 206. The minister shakes his head. He will prove to me that I am a case and a half out. Well, I will say that a great portion of the pack was not inspected, P.C. 206 is now in effect and it will be illegal to inspect that salmon unless somebody has taken an oath that they were landed at the wharf last August or September within twenty-four hours after being caught. See how absurd this is! Talk of being advised by the Justice depai'tment! That may have been so, but the advice was not according to common sense, beoause it is not common sense to say in February: you must, not on fish canned hereafter, but on fish inspected hereafter, produce a certificate in regard to something that happened six months previously. That cannot be done. What are you going to do-to break the law or ignore it? Admit the whole thing is a joke and drop it? Are you going to refuse perhaps 10,000, 50,000 or 100.000 cases a certificate altogether because this is the law? The law says that an inspector shall not give a certificate unless the fish have been landed within twenty-four hours

Supply-Fisheries
after 'having |been caught. This provision was not even dreamed of in January and the fish were packed long before that. I should like the minister to explain how he gets around that situation?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is not very well posted on the inspection which was practically completed before the regulation came into force. speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine

They were inspected not according to law.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine

If they were inspected after February 3, the packers would have to produce this certificate and they could not do so. The law has been flagrantly broken, and quite properly so, because it is no good and should not be in existence.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The hon. member
knows quite well that the regulation has no retroactive effect.
The order in council was passed on February 3 and on that date the pack was not inspected in full. What was done about that?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The regulation was not intended to apply to the catch of last year.

Why did it not say so, then? This regulation, involving the whole genius of the Justice department and the Fisheries department, was rushed through in a week and there was not time to consider it properly. It is a blot on the record of the Fisheries department.

This item affords an opportunity for a few general observations on this question of fisheries. We have so far heard a great deal from British Columbia and it might be in order if we gave our attention for a short time to the Atlantic coast fisheries. No other natural resource is capable of greater development than the Atlantic coast fisheries, and it is
about time the government took active measures to develop it. We now find, in going over the Atlantic coast, scenes of pitiful destitution among the fishermen. During the last forty or fifty years the fishing population of Nova Scotia has declined almost one-half, and the one-half that is left is living in the direst poverty. The causes of this condition are many. Many people wish to make the steam trawler responsible for the situation and to asoribe to its use all the ills that now affect the fishing population there. On that question I have a perfectly open mind. I am not interested one way or the other, but I doubt whether under the circumstances the present condition of those shore fishermen can be fairly attributed to the activities of the trawler. I do not think they can. As a matter of fact a great many trawlers from other countries fish in our waters outside the three mile limit, while I understand that our regulations call for our trawlers to fish outside the twelve mile -limit. So that from any point of view I do not think that the present condition of the fishermen can at any rate be wholly attributed to the operations of the trawler.
Those fishermen of ours are in a pitiable position. Their very desperate conditions have forced them to take some cooperative measures to try to make a living for themselves. They are forming little cooperative societies, but so far -they have not been able to do very much along that line, because, to start with they are very poor; they have no capital, and the storms that frequently ravage that coast clean up all their little plant, their boats and their nets.
There is now over four million dollars in the treasury of this country to the credit of the fishermen of the maritime provinces and Quebec. That money has been there for over fifty years. It was put there as a result of the Washington award. The money was paid as compensation for the privileges obtained by the American fishermen in our waters. The government of that day did not know what to do with the money. They got $4,500,000, and they kept half a million dollars for their costs and put $4,000,000 into the consolidated fund. It had no business ever to go there. That was a trust fund for the fishermen of the maritime provinces and Quebec. The government did not know what to do with it, and no government from that day to this has had wit enough to grapple with that question and deal justly with those fishermen. For fifty years now we have seen the spectacle of one government following another, and the
Supply-Fisheries

Department of Fisheries never in charge of a man who had wit enough to do justice to the fishermen of the maritime provinces and Quebec. The time has arrived when justice should be done. The fishermen need help and they must have it.
Some four or five years ago the late government appointed a commission beaded by the present president of the exchequer court, and that commission made a study of conditions in the maritime provinces and made a report and certain recommendations. In one recommendation they deal with this money that is to the credit of those fishermen in the dominion treasury, and which has been parcelled out by means of measly little fishing bounties, which was the only method which ever suggested itself to the government of that day, some fifty years ago. From that day to this we have never had in charge of the Fisheries department a man who could grapple with this question and settle it. I may say that we did have a serious hope when the present Minister of Finance took charge of that department, and during the short time he was there I am bound to say that a considerable improvement was made. So far the department has been under the administration of an acting minister who certainly has not been able to give it the attention which its importance deserves.
I have said that this $4,000,000 was placed in the consolidated fund, and the interest on it at four per cent, amounting to $160,000 a year, was parcelled out in the form of small bounty cheques to the fishermen according to the size of their boat-little cheques of five or six or seven dollars. The money was simply frittered away. The time has arrived now, after fifty years, when there must be some change made in that respect. As I have said, the fishermen down there are making valiant efforts for themselves to improve their conditions. Why cannot this money he devoted to helping them in their cooperative efforts, to enabling them to secure plant and bait and storage facilities for their fish? Surely the time has come to carry out the recommendation made by this commission some four or five years ago. Speaking of that $4,000,000, the commission said:
We recommend, however, that it is not applied to any of the purposes mentioned in the Deep Sea Fisheries Act, that is for bounties to boats, vessels and fishermen, but that it be specially devoted to such productive uses as assistance in the construction of brine freezing plants, fish meal plants, driers, bait and cold storage plants for organized groups of fishermen. or others engaged in any phase of the industry, upon proper terms and conditions,

and to such other substantial purposes as may appear desirable; the amount apportioned to Quebec and the maritime provinces should be in the proportions in which the Fishing Bounties were distributed in 1928.
There is a clear-cut recommendation from the commission appointed by the late government, but that recommendation has remained in abeyance from that day to this. In the meantime the fishermen have gone down from one strata of poverty to another, and neither this nor any other government has seen fit to adopt proper measures for dealing with this question. We need storage facilities. There was a cold storage plant at North Sydney, but it was destroyed by fire a few years ago. It now stands in need of repairs. It affords storage facilities for perhaps two or three hundred fishermen all along the coast of Victoria county and the county of Cape Breton, but it remains there in a state of dis-pair, having been destroyed by fire. Why? Simply because we cannot get $6,000 from this government to help repair it. It requires $18,000 to repair it and put it in shape, and fit it for storage. The town will give $6,000, the provincial government will give $6,000, and we are after this government to give the other $6,000. But so far we have not succeeded. The fishermen also require some assistance in the transporting of fresh lobsters to Boston. That transportation has been afforded to certain districts, but it has not been afforded to the districts in the county that I represent.
The fishermen down there also want certain changes made in the regulations governing lobster fishing. They are told by the department that they do not know what they are talking about, that the officials here know more about lobster fishing than the fishermen themselves do.
I submit to the government with all the earnestness of which I am capable that this year should see an earnest effort made by the department to put into effect the recommendation made by the royal commission on fisheries to which I have referred. I know that the fishermen of the maritime provinces would be inspired with a great hope if the minister to-night would give us any reason to believe that the matter to which I have referred will receive consideration in the coming summer, and that active steps will be taken to carry out the report of the commission headed by the president of the exchequer court.

Mr. Chairman, I have only
one more matter to bring before the committee, and then the minister may requiescat

Supply-Fisheries
in pace. I wish to repeat the protest I made about eleven months ago to-day concerning the Vancouver offices of 'the minister's department. I shall not repeat what I said on the former occasion; it appears in Hansard of May 21, 1932. In these days of excessive economy, when taxation is so severe, it is doubly necessary to be very careful to avoid unnecessary expenditures. A new psychology is growing up. People used to think: "Oh well, Bill has a job with the government; it is all right. It does not matter very much whether he does anything or not." But now they are thinking differently. Men stop me on the street and say: "Why is so and so paid for doing so and so? The expenditure is not justified; it is only a half time job" -and so on. For those reasons we must review these matters.
On the Pacific coast in the last two or three years there has been a tremendous falling off in the salmon industry. There has been a big drop in the number of plants, in the boats employed and in the catch. I have records before me which show that last year only thirty-five canneries were operating, but that two years before, seventy-five were operating, or more than double the number. Last year there were 2,180 fewer fishing licences issued than were issued in 1930. A bulletin issued by the minister's department in the month of March contains the information that for the month of February forty tons of fish were caught in British Columbia waters while in the February two years earlier one hundred and thirty-three tons were caught. Forty tons is not a very large quantity-only about one and a half tons a day. But to take out that forty tons of fish the services of eleven clerical officials were required in the head office. I am not referring to the numerous minor officials, but to the clerical staff at head office. Eleven officials were required to superintend the catching o.f a ton and a half of fish each day.
No doubt the chief supervisor out there got his instructions, as everyone did two years ago, to cut down expenses. He did cut them down, but he cut them at the wrong end. Expenses divide themselves into two heads, one overhead and the other the work actually done on the ground. One would naturally expect, with so many fewer canneries, boats, and fishermen, that the clerical staff would be greatly decreased. However, it was not. The work actually done on the ground is done by the air force, which was cut thirty per cent, the patrol boats, which were cut twenty-seven per cent-and I am
not talking about the protective service, which consists of two big steamers, but am directing my remarks to the small patrol boats on the ground-and the guardians, which were cut down forty-three per cent. Those are the services for which we spend $400,000.
As I have said, the air force, the patrol boats and the guardians were cut down in the manner I have indicated. But what was done with the overhead? A few days ago I obtained a return from the government. While it is somewhat obscure it indicates that there are thirteen officials in the office, and that there were thirteen in 1930. The report shows fifteen, but two held temporary positions. We see therefore that the staff is the same size. I look at the Ottawa office of the Department of Fisheries and I find that they have been cut down from eighty-nine to sixty-five or about twenty-four per cent. But the Vancouver office numbers were not cut down. In fact, some of the salaries were raised; the chief supervisor gets S180 more than he did before. He now gets $720 a year more than the same officer in the mari-times, despite the fact that the maritimes officer has three provinces to take care of. I see other increases in salaries also-not decreases, but increases. I see that there are seven officials and six stenographers, or practically a stenographer for each official. I know of no office in Canada where that principle prevails. I glanced over the figures for a number of departments which have been before us in the last few weeks, and I find that the number of officials for each stenographer runs from four to twenty. I cannot find any instance where there were less than four officials to one stenographer, but in British Columbia we have a stenographer for each official. I suppose she puts her lily-white hand on his fevered brow and gets him a glass of water occasionally.
Order.
That is disgraceful.

I see that the district supervisor and chief supervisor are in the same office. There is another supervisor thirteen miles away. There are five supervisors in British Columbia, two of whom are in the head office and one thirteen miles away. Then we come to the principal statistical clerk. Mr. Chairman, after listening to the discussion which took place in connection with the Atlantic and Pacific coast fisheries, I think it pertinent to-now refer to those of central Canada. Two years ago the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) practically promised that the inquiry begun in 1930, would be continued in 1931 and 1932. I am alluding to the fisheries of Hudson bay and James bay. We are satisfied that it is possible to develop the fisheries of that part of the country. Both the inquiry and survey or patrolling carried on in 1930 and 1931 did not prove satisfactory and I have already complained of the fact. The Department of Fisheries is no doubt aware that companies were formed last year and started fishing operations. These will further develop this year. I would therefore request that the hon. Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Duranleau)-

Supply-Fisheries
assure me that the inquiry begun two or three years ago will be continued, and if possible, completed this year. We are far from being satisfied with the report of the inquiry stating that no sea fish inhabit the waters of Hudson bay or James bay. The Ontario provincial government has extended its railway from Cochrane to Moose Factory or Moosonee. As recently as last year the provincial government inaugurated this new service. This proves that the provincial government intends to give a good railway service to central Canada.
As I intimated two years ago to the hon. Minister of Finance, there are people in our section of the country, under the impression that some prejudice exists against developing the fisheries of central Canada, because it is feared that an unfair competition will result against the fisheries existing in eastern and western Canada. I do not believe in such fears. However, if the government persists in its attitude and does not hold a more thorough inquiry so as to bring out the facts as regards the fisheries of central Canada, I shall be led to believe that there is some truth in such an assertion. I have faith in the progressive spirit which animates the Minister of Fisheries; I hope he realizes what the development of these fisheries means to New Ontario, and to that section of the country, and that he will continue the inquiry so auspiciously started three years ago.
As it was stated by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Willis) and the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Stitt), who so well represent their constituents in the house, we are convinced, having personal knowledge of the facts, that sea fish actually thrive in that vast interior sea. Nature certainly did not create such a large body of water without providing for potential fisheries, capable of being exploited with profit by those who might wish to invest their capital in such an enterprise. I may inform the minister that a large number of people are willing to invest considerable amounts to develop such fisheries. Previous to closing my remarks, may I state that, knowing the spirit of initiative of the minister of fisheries, I trust he will fully acquiesce in the wish of the people of that section of the country and that the study of this question will be carried out more efficiently than in the past. I regret to state that within the last two years, nothing was done in this connection. However, I hope that next summer the government will find it
possible to continue this inquiry which, I have no doubt, will amply prove, as we contend in our section of the country, that our fisheries can compete, both as to quantity and quality, with those of other parts of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I
listened to my hon. friend with much interest and I wish to congratulate him on the optimism he displays as regards the fisheries of his section of the country. As to the inquiry held in 1931, I understand that it was completed. I do not wish to state that we shall not make further inquiry in this matter in order to meet the wishes of my hon. friend; however I cannot make any promise for this year. All are aware that the department must practise economy; should we decide that further inquiry must be carried out, we shall have the necessary appropriation placed in the estimates next year; however, for the present, I cannot pledge the department to any definite action in the matter.
